tracks.title: Software that works unwatched
tracks.text: Lesson zero two point seven — telemetry. A sub-lesson, under the nexus. [curious] Here's the situation. You run things that work while you're not looking — keepers overnight, agents on a schedule, a workflow that fires at nine. And the next morning, the only question that matters is small… and unanswerable in most stacks. What did it actually do? The industry's answer to that question is a zoo. Stdout in one place… app logs in another… traces in a third… metrics in a fourth… a dashboard bolted over all of it… and a bill at the end of the month. You don't get an answer. You get five partial answers, in five shapes — and the work of reconciling them is yours. And for agents it's worse. Because the interesting unit isn't a request — it's a tool call. And half of those moves happen inside a sandbox you cannot print from. [sighs] The most observable-hungry collaborator you've ever run… is the one you can see the least.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Telemetry, here, is one event shape — a tool-call record of nine fields — written at one chokepoint… appended to one file per run… where every observer is a reader of those lines, never a second logger. [curious] The whole design is in that last clause. There is one grammar of signal — the tool-call event — and many literacies. The summary command reads it. The website wire reads it. The dream digest reads it. The ledger seals it. Nothing exports a second format, because nothing needs to. So what are the nine fields? Let me walk them. First… step — a counter for this run. Second… agent — which worker took the step, the agent's name, or nothing for a singleton. Third… tool — the tool's name. Fourth… args — the call's arguments, a path or a query or a url. Fifth… output — the result, but sliced down, two hundred characters in the file. A record, not a transcript. Sixth… exit code. Seventh… error, or nothing. Eighth… duration in milliseconds. And ninth… a timestamp. That file is called underscore steps dot jsonl — one JSON line per tool call, appended for the life of the run. [excited] And everything else on this page… is a way of reading it.

tracks.title: The chokepoint
tracks.text: Now — the chokepoint. The reason nothing escapes is structural. The event isn't built by the caller… and it isn't optional. It's assembled and appended at a single function, inside the tool-call loop, fired for every step — regardless of any hook the caller passed in. A caller can subscribe to the live feed. A caller cannot opt a step out of the record. The phrase in the source is exact — nothing escapes by construction. Picture the flow. The model calls a tool. The loop wraps that call in a one-hundred-fifty-second ceiling… runs it… and then appends one event to the file, lock-free. If anyone is watching, the same event also goes to the subscriber — but that's a bonus. The append always happens. And here's the detail that earns the morning's trust. Every tool call is bounded at a hundred and fifty seconds. [curious] So a wedged tool doesn't stall forever and vanish. It times out — and the timeout becomes a tool-error event, like any other. A hang is data… not a black hole. Which is why the summary you read in the morning is complete… even when last night went badly.

tracks.title: Three writers, one grammar
tracks.text: Three writers… one grammar. This is the part that makes the rest free. An agent doesn't only call native tools. It calls toolkit commands across the Dock membrane… and it runs work inside the WASM sandbox. Three different worlds, with three different boundaries. And all three write the same file… in the same shape. Picture three lanes pouring into one funnel. First lane… native agent tools — tool name, shell, or read, or fetch. Second lane… Dock command calls — tool name, command colon, then the command's name. Third lane… WASM spans — tool name, wasm colon, then the span's name. All three drop the same nine fields into one file — underscore steps dot jsonl. And out the bottom, four readers drink from it — the summary, the activity wire, the dream digest, and the signed ledger. The convergence is the whole trick. A Dock command writes its own exit code and timing — and the workdir it writes to is held in host context, so a guest inside the sandbox never sees the path and can't aim a write at the log. [excited] And because all three land the same shape in the same file, the reader that rolls up a run needs zero new query code to count a sandboxed command the same as a native one. One grammar in. One read out. Now — one honest note. The WASM-span lane is a complete host sink… but it isn't wired end to end yet. There's no telemetry capability for a guest to call it through… and no test exercises it. The feasibility spike confirmed nested spans roll up correctly — a two-call run summing to forty milliseconds. But the guest-side tooling is the blocker. We'd rather mark that clearly… than imply the sandbox is already narrating itself.

tracks.title: The read stack
tracks.text: Next — the read stack. Once the lines exist, observing is just reading them at different altitudes. Let me give you the five readers. First… summary — it answers, what happened in this one run? It rolls up stage, tool calls, total time, errors, and the last fifteen steps — by reading the file directly, so it works mid-flight, with no database. Second… index — it answers, what ran lately, across sessions? A pure scan, newest first — so it costs nothing, and it can't drift from the truth, because it has no truth of its own. Third… persist — the durable per-run SQLite database, written once at run end, single writer, no contention. Fourth… the activity wire — what's it doing right now, for the public — anonymous, read-only, the last few lines, slimmed. And fifth… the stream — a WebSocket that pushes a frame per step as it happens. Now let me read you the loop you'll actually live in. You type, wbx telemetry, and you get a little table — slug, stage, calls, errors, milliseconds. One row reads, wulu refresh, done, forty-two calls, zero errors. Another reads, brand run, error, seventeen calls, three errors. So you ask about that bad one — wbx telemetry, brand run. And it tells you — stage error, seventeen calls, three errors. And then it names the wounds. Step nine, shell — tool timeout. Step eleven, fetch — exit one. [curious] There it is. The failing run, named. The two bad steps, quoted. The timeout from that hundred-fifty-second bound, showing up exactly where the chokepoint promised it would. No dashboard. No integration. One command, reading one file. And riding on the same feed — the activity wire tails the last few lines for a public watcher, slimmed to a tool, a target, a time, and an agent. And the thoughts narration — eight words, generated lazily, only when someone is actually watching.

tracks.title: Record becomes memory
tracks.text: And here the record becomes something logs never are — memory. After a run, a sleep phase digests the recent telemetry, the git log, and the backlog… into a single journal entry. And the agent reads its newest entry when it next wakes. So last night's trace isn't a graveyard of lines — it's the thing the next run orients against. Picture the handoff. A run ends. A gather step takes the last twenty-five steps, the git log, and the plan… and hands them to a small model. The model writes one org entry, under five fixed headings — tale, goals, blue sky, fears, verdicts, and carry. And the next waking run reads that entry first… and resumes from carry, instead of re-reading the world. The transformation is concrete. Each of those twenty-five lines is reformatted to a terse move — shell, wb toolkit verify rss, exit zero. The verdict lines — pick up, put down, cancel — are applied mechanically to the plan board. And carry is the resume-state the next run reads. [curious] The cadence is deliberate, too. A full dream only fires after an audit commit, and at least fifty minutes since the last. A lighter daydream — forty words, never committed — fires every twelve minutes or so, from just the last six tool names. The agent reads its newest dream at orient time. It never writes one. Sleeping and waking are separate jobs… and telemetry is the bridge between them. The full story lives in the dreaming lesson.

tracks.title: Record becomes proof
tracks.text: Record becomes proof. The same file that feeds memory can be sealed. And the ledger doesn't write a second log — it computes a seal over the one the telemetry already wrote. Picture a chain. You take the raw bytes of underscore steps dot jsonl. Each line is hashed into the next — hash of the previous, joined with this line — starting from a genesis string, workbooks ledger v one. That gives you a chain. Then the head of the chain is signed with the tenant's key. And out comes a small ledger file. Verification returns two facts. First… tamper-evident — no line was changed. Second… attributable — this agent, this key, signed it. Plus the count and the head. [excited] It's the same wb ledger command from the read stack — sealed automatically at the end of a workflow run. The seal lives over the log… not beside it. And the ledger lesson owns the full story.

tracks.title: Record becomes self-extension
tracks.text: And the last transformation closes a loop — record becomes self-extension. When an agent hits a wall — its toolkit can't do the thing — it doesn't stall, and it doesn't fake success. It files an issue, with one field that matters — tried. The evidence of the wall, which is exactly a telemetry-shaped trace of what failed. Picture the path. An agent hits a wall, carrying its failing trace. It calls file issue. That lands in the autopoet's backlog — org files, with duplicates from the same tenant bumping a seen count instead of re-filing. The autopoet picks the most-seen issue first, and works it. And then a gate — wb toolkit verify. If it passes, the issue goes done. If it can't be verified, it gets downgraded back to open. [curious] And here's the part that matters for this page. The autopoet's own run goes through the same agent path — so its steps land in the same file, in the same grammar, stamped agent, autopoet. The system that extends the system… is observable by the same telemetry it observes. The full account is the autopoet lesson's. This page only owes you the seam.

tracks.title: The second lane
tracks.text: Now — the second lane. There's a second stream of signal that is deliberately not the step grammar — because it answers a different question. Ops metering. Every broker decision — every allow or deny of a capability request — increments an atomic counter, keyed by broker and outcome. And denials land in a small forensics ring, the last hundred and twenty-eight, with the guest-controlled target truncated, so a hostile component can't exhaust memory through the audit itself. But here's the important move, at the boundary. Alongside its own counters, the broker audit emits a standard Erlang telemetry event — broker, outcome, reason, target. That's the well-known contract the whole BEAM ecosystem already speaks. So Prometheus, a SIEM, an APM — they can attach to the engine's security signal… without coupling to any internal layout. [curious] The step grammar is for you, reading your own runs. This lane is where the engine's signal meets the outside monitoring world… on the world's terms.

tracks.title: Private by default
tracks.text: Private by default. All of this telemetry is intensely personal — it's the minute-by-minute record of how your agent thinks. So the rule is one sentence. Sharing exposes work… never the session that produced it. One module owns that boundary — and every egress path, git, bundle, library, consults it before anything leaves the machine. There are five of these sidecar files, and not one of them ever ships. First… the step log itself — written on every tool call. Second… a status file — running, done, or error. Third… a slim per-step trace. Fourth… the run-end SQLite database. And fifth… the signed ledger seal. None of them travel when you share. And the boundary isn't a list someone maintains — it's a pattern. An underscore prefix, paired with a json or a database suffix, catches every sidecar here… and any future one the same way. So a new telemetry file is private the day it's invented. [excited] The same module auto-writes a git-ignore, which makes git add everything safe by default. You cannot accidentally commit your own session. When you share a workbook… the work goes, and the diary stays.

tracks.title: What it isn't
tracks.text: The honest part — what it isn't. In full. First… the WASM-span lane is a complete host sink, with no guest wiring yet. The spike confirmed it works. The guest-side tooling is the blocker. Treat sandbox self-narration as confirmed-feasible… not shipped. Second… the file is a record, not a transcript. Outputs are sliced to two hundred characters — enough to know what a step did and whether it worked, not enough to replay it. Third… workflow runs index under an ephemeral path. The live summary is real and free — but it's reading a working directory, not a warehouse. The durable copy is the run-end database and the sealed ledger. Fourth… the step grammar is not an OpenTelemetry exporter. Only the broker lane emits the standard events. And fifth… the log is editable until sealed. Its tamper-evidence comes from the ledger's hash chain, applied at run end — not from the append itself. And last, the most important one. None of this ever leaves your machine. This is your telemetry — the record you read to understand your own software — not product analytics, not a phone-home, not a metric we collect. [curious] The privacy isn't a setting. It's the default the whole egress path enforces.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I watch a run live? Yes — two ways. The summary rolls up a run even mid-flight, because it reads the file directly and needs no finished database. And the stream is a WebSocket that pushes a frame per step. Does my telemetry leave my machine? No. Private by construction — one module gates every egress path, and the naming pattern keeps the files out of git, bundles, and the library. There's no collection, no phone-home. How do I hook up Prometheus? Through the second lane — the broker audit emits standard Erlang telemetry events, the contract the BEAM ecosystem already speaks. Can the agent fake its own log? The append is at one chokepoint, fired for every step — so a step can't quietly skip itself. The raw file is editable after the fact, which is exactly why the ledger exists. [chuckles] Trust the seal, not the file. And — why one file, instead of proper logs, traces, and metrics? Because for agent work, the interesting unit is the tool call — and one event shape captures it whole. Split it across three subsystems and you've bought three formats to reconcile. One file means the summary, the wire, the dream, and the ledger are all just readers. No drift between copies… because there's only one copy.

tracks.title: Back up to the nexus
tracks.text: So that's telemetry. One event shape… one chokepoint… one file per run. And every observer — the summary, the activity wire, the dream, the signed ledger — is just a reader of the same lines. Nothing escapes… because the writer sits inside the loop, not beside it. [curious] This was a sub-lesson under the nexus — the engine watching itself. The way back up is short. The nexus, lesson zero two, for the engine this all runs on. And from here, three transformations are worth following — the autopoet, where a recorded wall becomes a new capability… dreaming, where telemetry becomes memory… and the ledger, where the same lines become proof. One grammar of signal. Many literacies. That's the whole idea.
